records.topic: The Grid That Came 4 Minutes From Collapse
records.coreQuestion: How close did Texas come to a total grid collapse in 2021?
records.openingLine: Why Texas's grid came 4 minutes from collapse.
records.secondBeat: In 2021, frozen plants dropped supply far below demand.
records.dependency: Grid stability depends on enough generation reserve to hold frequency when supply suddenly drops.
records.mechanism: When generation falls below demand, frequency drops; operators must shed load fast to stop plants tripping.
records.bottleneck: Freezing weather knocked out generation faster than reserves could cover.
records.failureConsequence: Had frequency kept falling, the grid could have needed a full black start lasting weeks.
records.resilience: Rolling outages shed load and kept the grid from collapsing entirely.
records.expectedConsequence: millions lose power for days to save the grid
editorialTitles: How Close Texas Came to Total Blackout
Why Grids Shed Load to Survive

facts.claim: According to ERCOT, the Texas power grid was four minutes and 37 seconds away from complete failure when partial grid shutdowns were implemented.
More than 4.5 million homes and businesses were left without power, some for several days.
Damages due to the cold wave and winter storm were estimated to be at least $26.5 billion, one of the most expensive disasters in the state's history.
In February 2021, the state of Texas suffered a major power crisis.
By February 19, the number was updated to at least 32 people who died.

narration.text: Why Texas's grid came 4 minutes from collapse.
In 2021, frozen plants dropped supply far below demand.
The margin was four minutes and 37 seconds.
Operators cut power to millions to keep frequency up.
More than 4.5 million homes and businesses went dark.
Damages reached at least $26.5 billion.
That's why reserves decide whether a grid bends or breaks.

records.coreQuestion: What happened when attackers shot up a California substation, and why are transformers so hard to replace?
records.openingLine: Why gunmen shot 17 transformers in one night.
records.secondBeat: In 2013, attackers hit California's Metcalf substation.
records.dependency: Substations depend on large transformers that are custom-built and slow to replace.
records.mechanism: Transformers step voltage up and down; cooling oil keeps them running, and losing it forces shutdown.
records.bottleneck: Large transformers are custom units with long lead times.
records.failureConsequence: Damage to several at once can take a substation out for weeks.
records.resilience: Rerouting power through other substations avoided outages at Metcalf.
records.expectedConsequence: costly damage even when the lights stay on
editorialTitles: The Substation Attack That Woke Up the Grid
Why Transformers Are the Grid's Weak Spot

facts.claim: On April 16, 2013, an attack was carried out on Pacific Gas and Electric Company's Metcalf transmission substation in Coyote, California.
The attack, in which gunmen fired on 17 electrical transformers, resulted in more than $15 million worth of equipment damage, but it had little impact on the station's electrical power supply.
More than 100 expended 7.62×39mm cases were later found at the site.
Some customers of Level 3 Communications, an Internet service provider, lost service.

narration.text: Why gunmen shot 17 transformers in one night.
In 2013, attackers hit California's Metcalf substation.
They left more than 100 bullet casings behind.
The damage topped $15 million.
Grid operators rerouted power, so few lights went out.
Big transformers are custom-built, with long waits for replacements.
That's why the grid's weak spot is sitting behind a fence.

records.coreQuestion: What does it take to run one of the world's biggest battery plants safely?
records.openingLine: Why one battery site stores 2,500 megawatt-hours.
records.secondBeat: Moss Landing can deliver 630 megawatts at once.
records.dependency: Grids increasingly depend on giant battery plants to shift solar power into the evening.
records.mechanism: Thousands of battery modules charge and discharge through inverters, cooled and monitored constantly.
records.bottleneck: Thermal management failures can take large blocks of storage offline.
records.failureConsequence: Fires and overheating incidents have shut sections of the plant.
records.resilience: Separate phases and facilities keep some storage running during incidents.
records.expectedConsequence: stored capacity disappears when a site goes offline
visualScenes: fire response at a battery site
editorialTitles: Inside One of the World's Biggest Batteries
Why Battery Plants Live or Die by Cooling

facts.claim: As of 2025, the site's battery storage facility is one of the largest in the world, at 630 MW (power) and 2,500 MWh (energy).
In September 2021 Phase 1 was shut down after a high temperature safety incident (no fire) caused by a leak in a liquid cooling hose, while Phase 2 kept operating.
On September 20, 2022, a fire occurred at the Elkhorn Battery Facility when a single Tesla Megapack caught fire.
Commercial generation started in 1950 with a capacity of 613 MW.
When completed in 2002, the plant was the largest power plant in California by capacity, at 2560 MW.

narration.text: Why one battery site stores 2,500 megawatt-hours.
Moss Landing can deliver 630 megawatts at once.
It shifts daytime power into the evening peak.
In 2021, a leaking cooling hose shut down Phase 1.
In 2022, a single Megapack caught fire at a neighbouring site.
The site once hosted California's largest power plant, at 2,560 megawatts.
Cooling and monitoring keep every module in its safe range.
That's why grid batteries are really heat-management plants.

records.topic: The Stuck Valve Behind Three Mile Island
records.coreQuestion: How did a stuck valve and a misread signal lead to a partial meltdown?
records.openingLine: Why 6% leftover heat nearly melted a reactor.
records.secondBeat: In 1979, Three Mile Island's reactor shut down automatically.
records.dependency: Reactors depend on continuous coolant flow to remove heat, even after shutdown.
records.mechanism: After a trip, decay heat still needs removing; relief valves and pumps must work as indicated.
records.bottleneck: Operators trusted an indicator that showed the valve closed when it was open.
records.failureConsequence: Coolant escaped, the core overheated and partially melted.
records.resilience: Containment held most radioactivity; operator training and instrumentation were overhauled.
visualScenes: cooling towers at Three Mile Island
editorialTitles: The Valve That Caused Three Mile Island
Why Reactors Need Cooling After Shutdown

facts.claim: The main chain of events leading to the partial core meltdown on Wednesday, March 28, 1979, began at 4:00:36 a.m.
The reactor continued to generate decay heat, initially equivalent to approximately 6% of the pre-trip power level.
When RCS pressure rose to 2,255 psi (155.5 bar), the pilot-operated relief valve (PORV) opened, relieving steam through piping to the reactor coolant drain tank.
Cleanup at TMI-2 started in August 1979 and officially ended in December 1993, with a total cost of about $1 billion.

narration.text: Why 6% leftover heat nearly melted a reactor.
In 1979, Three Mile Island's reactor shut down automatically.
But decay heat kept coming, about 6% of full power.
A relief valve opened to vent pressure, and stuck.
Operators believed it was closed.
Coolant drained away, and the core partly melted.
Cleanup lasted until 1993 and cost about $1 billion.
That's why cooling after shutdown matters as much as control.

records.topic: The Network Running 75% of Active Satellites
records.coreQuestion: How did one company end up operating most of the active satellites in orbit?
records.openingLine: Why one company flies 75% of active satellites.
records.secondBeat: Starlink had about 10,413 satellites by June 2026.
records.dependency: Broadband users in remote areas, ships and aircraft increasingly depend on low-orbit constellations.
records.mechanism: Thousands of satellites relay traffic between users and ground stations, and to each other by laser.
records.bottleneck: One operator runs most active manoeuvrable satellites in orbit.
records.failureConsequence: An outage or policy change at one company affects users across 160 countries.
records.resilience: Competing constellations and terrestrial networks remain alternatives.
records.expectedConsequence: connectivity for remote users hinges on one provider
visualScenes: train of satellites crossing the night sky
user dish on a remote cabin
editorialTitles: The Constellation That Took Over Orbit
Why One Network Runs Most Active Satellites

facts.claim: As of June 2026, the network consisted of approximately 10,413 satellites (10,397 operational) in low Earth orbit.
Starlink accounts for approximately 75% of all active maneuverable satellites in Earth orbit and had more than 12 million subscribers as of June 2026.
Starlink provides broadband Internet service in approximately 160 countries and territories.
The inter-satellite laser links were successfully tested in late 2020.
SpaceX began launching Starlink satellites in 2019.

narration.text: Why one company flies 75% of active satellites.
Starlink had about 10,413 satellites by June 2026.
It served more than 12 million subscribers.
It reaches about 160 countries and territories.
Laser links between satellites were tested in 2020.
That much orbital capacity now sits with a single operator.
That's why low orbit has become critical infrastructure.

records.topic: The Bridge Collapse That Closed a Port for 11 Weeks
records.coreQuestion: How did one ship striking a bridge close a major U.S. port for weeks?
records.openingLine: Why Baltimore's port closed for 11 weeks.
records.secondBeat: A ship struck the Key Bridge, dropping it into the channel.
records.dependency: The Port of Baltimore depends on one navigable channel under the Key Bridge site.
records.mechanism: Ships reach the port through a dredged channel; wreckage in it blocks deep-draft traffic.
records.bottleneck: A single channel serves the whole port.
records.failureConsequence: After the collapse, most shipping stopped until salvage crews cleared the channel.
records.resilience: Temporary channels let smaller vessels pass while salvage continued.
records.expectedConsequence: cargo diverts to other ports at millions of dollars a day
visualScenes: collapsed bridge spans in the channel
container ship with wreckage on its bow
editorialTitles: The Bridge Collapse That Shut a Port
Why One Channel Decides a Port's Fate

facts.claim: The collapse blocked most shipping to and from the Port of Baltimore for 11 weeks.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse

facts.claim: The economic impact of the closure of the waterway was estimated at $15 million per day.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse

facts.claim: The port had been the leading port for automobiles and light trucks for 13 straight years, handling more than 847,000 vehicles in 2023.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse

facts.claim: In 2023, the port handled more than 444,000 passengers and 52.3 million tons of foreign cargo valued at $80 billion.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse

narration.text: Why Baltimore's port closed for 11 weeks.
A ship struck the Key Bridge, dropping it into the channel.
The port had led the U.S. in car shipments for 13 years.
In 2023, it handled more than 847,000 vehicles.
It moved 52.3 million tons of foreign cargo in 2023.
The closure cost an estimated $15 million per day.
Salvage crews had to clear the channel piece by piece.
That's why a port is only as open as its channel.

records.topic: The 2,750 Tonnes Stored Beside a City
records.coreQuestion: How did a forgotten cargo of ammonium nitrate destroy much of a city's port?
records.openingLine: Why 2,750 tonnes waited in Beirut's port.
records.secondBeat: The ammonium nitrate reached Beirut by ship in 2013.
records.dependency: Port safety depends on tracking dangerous goods and removing them promptly.
records.mechanism: Hazardous cargo must be declared, stored safely and removed; abandoned cargo can sit for years.
records.bottleneck: Seized cargo stayed in a port warehouse for years without resolution.
records.failureConsequence: A fire ignited the stockpile, causing one of history's largest non-nuclear explosions.
records.resilience: Stronger rules on storage and disposal of seized hazardous cargo followed.
records.expectedConsequence: a port and neighbourhoods destroyed in seconds
editorialTitles: The Forgotten Cargo That Destroyed Beirut's Port
Why Dangerous Goods Can't Be Left Waiting

facts.claim: On 4 August 2020, a major explosion occurred in Beirut, Lebanon, caused by the ignition of 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate.
The explosion resulted in at least 218 deaths, 7,000 injuries, and approximately 300,000 displaced people, alongside property damage estimated at US$15 billion.
A consignment was transported aboard the MV Rhosus vessel in August 2013, carrying approximately 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate; on 21 November 2013, the ship made port in Beirut.
Its effects were felt in Lebanon and neighbouring regions, including Syria, Israel, and Cyprus, over 240 km (150 mi) away.

narration.text: Why 2,750 tonnes waited in Beirut's port.
The ammonium nitrate reached Beirut by ship in 2013.
It stayed stored in the port, beside the city.
In 2020, a fire set it off.
At least 218 people died and about 300,000 were displaced.
The blast was felt over 240 kilometres away.
That's why dangerous cargo needs a deadline, not just a label.

records.topic: The Malware That Froze a Shipping Giant
records.coreQuestion: How did malware in a small accounting program cripple global companies and ports?
records.openingLine: Why one software update cost Maersk $300 million.
records.secondBeat: In 2017, NotPetya spread through a Ukrainian accounting program.
records.dependency: Shipping lines and terminals depend on IT systems to book cargo and move containers.
records.mechanism: Terminal and booking systems run on corporate networks; malware spreading across them halts operations.
records.bottleneck: One compromised software update spread into networks worldwide.
records.failureConsequence: Terminals and bookings stopped until systems were rebuilt.
records.resilience: Offline backups and manual processes restored operations over days.
records.expectedConsequence: ports slow to manual paperwork while systems are rebuilt
editorialTitles: The Cyberattack That Froze a Shipping Giant
Why Ports Run on Software

facts.claim: On 27 June 2017, a software update was distributed via M.E.Doc's update server, after which reports of the NotPetya ransomware attack began to appear.
Estimated damages to specific companies included over US$870 million to Merck, US$400 million to FedEx, US$384 million to Saint-Gobain, and US$300 million to Maersk.
ESET estimated on 28 June 2017 that 80% of all infections were in Ukraine, with Germany second hardest hit with about 9%.
Estimates suggest that M.E.Doc had about 400,000 customers across Ukraine, covering approximately 90% of domestic firms.

narration.text: Why one software update cost Maersk $300 million.
In 2017, NotPetya spread through a Ukrainian accounting program.
That program served about 90% of Ukrainian firms.
It also hit Merck for over $870 million.
FedEx lost about $400 million.
Terminals and bookings ran on the same infected networks.
That's why modern ports can be stopped without touching a ship.

records.topic: The Pumps That Left 150,000 People Without Water
records.coreQuestion: How did failing pumps leave a state capital without safe water?
records.openingLine: Why 150,000 people lost safe water in 2022.
records.secondBeat: Jackson, Mississippi's water system failed after flooding.
records.dependency: City water supply depends on treatment plants and pumps that push water into the network.
records.mechanism: High-lift pumps send treated water into mains; if they fail, pressure collapses citywide.
records.bottleneck: Aging plants with deferred maintenance had little redundancy.
records.failureConsequence: Flooding and pump failures left about 150,000 residents without safe water.
records.resilience: Emergency pumps, bottled water and federal funding followed.
records.expectedConsequence: boil-water notices and dry taps across a city
editorialTitles: How Jackson Lost Its Water
Why Old Pumps Can Leave a City Dry

facts.claim: A public health crisis in and around the city of Jackson, Mississippi, began in late August 2022 after the Pearl River flooded due to severe storms in the state.
This resulted in approximately 150,000 residents of the city being left without access to safe drinking water.
City leaders asked the state for $47 million for sewer repairs, but received only $3 million.
In December 2021, the Environmental Protection Agency announced an allocation of $74.9 million from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to Mississippi for water infrastructure improvements.

narration.text: Why 150,000 people lost safe water in 2022.
Jackson, Mississippi's water system failed after flooding.
Treatment plant pumps keep pressure in every pipe.
When they faltered, taps ran dry or unsafe.
The city had asked for $47 million for sewer repairs.
It received just $3 million.
That's why deferred maintenance becomes a public health crisis.

records.topic: The Oil Hidden in 70% of Personal Care Products
records.coreQuestion: Why is one tropical oil in most shampoos, soaps and snacks?
records.openingLine: Why 70% of beauty products hide palm oil.
records.secondBeat: Soap, shampoo, makeup and lotion all rely on it.
records.dependency: Food, cosmetics and biodiesel depend heavily on palm oil refined in a few countries.
records.mechanism: Crude palm oil is refined and fractionated into ingredients with hundreds of different names.
records.bottleneck: Indonesia alone produces about 60% of the world's palm oil.
records.failureConsequence: Export restrictions from a top producer ripple into food and cosmetics prices.
records.resilience: Other vegetable oils can substitute, at higher cost.
records.expectedConsequence: cooking oil and packaged food prices rise
editorialTitles: The Oil in Almost Everything
Why One Country Shapes Palm Oil Prices

facts.claim: Palm oil accounted for about 36% of global oils produced from oil crops in 2017.
The biggest global producers of palm oil are Indonesia, which produced 60% of it in 2022, followed by Malaysia, Thailand, and Nigeria.
Around 70% of personal care products including soap, shampoo, makeup, and lotion, contain ingredients derived from palm oil.
There are more than 200 different names for these palm oil ingredients and only 10% of them include the word palm.

narration.text: Why 70% of beauty products hide palm oil.
Soap, shampoo, makeup and lotion all rely on it.
It made up about 36% of crop oils in 2017.
Indonesia produced 60% of the world's supply in 2022.
It hides behind more than 200 ingredient names.
When a top producer restricts exports, prices jump worldwide.
That's why your bathroom shelf depends on refineries in Southeast Asia.

records.topic: The 180 Billion Cans Made Every Year
records.coreQuestion: Why is the humble drink can the biggest single use of aluminium?
records.openingLine: Why the world makes 180 billion cans.
records.secondBeat: Cans are the largest single use of aluminium.
records.dependency: Beverage makers depend on high-speed can lines and a steady supply of aluminium sheet.
records.mechanism: Can lines stamp, draw and coat aluminium into billions of thin-walled cans.
records.bottleneck: Can supply depends on aluminium sheet capacity and recycling rates.
records.failureConsequence: Shortages of cans or sheet ripple into drink supply.
records.resilience: Recycling returns aluminium to production quickly.
records.expectedConsequence: drink makers compete for scarce cans
editorialTitles: The Can Factory Behind Every Soda
Why Drink Cans Are Aluminium's Biggest Use

facts.claim: The global production amount of aluminum cans is 180 billion units annually and constitutes the largest single use of aluminum globally.
Cans are the most recycled beverage container, at a rate of 69% worldwide.
In 2012, 92% of the aluminum beverage cans sold in Switzerland were recycled.
Roughly $700 million worth of cans end up in landfills each year in the US.

narration.text: Why the world makes 180 billion cans.
Cans are the largest single use of aluminium.
About 69% are recycled worldwide.
Switzerland recycled 92% of its cans in 2012.
In the U.S., about $700 million worth hit landfills each year.
Every can line depends on a steady flow of aluminium sheet.
That's why recycling is part of the drink supply chain.

records.topic: The Chemical Made at 260 Million Tonnes a Year
records.coreQuestion: Why is sulfuric acid one of the most important chemicals nobody talks about?
records.openingLine: Why we make 260 million tonnes of acid.
records.dependency: Fertilizer, copper mining and many industries depend on sulfuric acid supply.
records.mechanism: Sulfur is burned to sulfur dioxide, oxidised to trioxide and absorbed into acid.
records.bottleneck: Supply depends heavily on sulfur recovered from oil and gas refining.
records.failureConsequence: Acid shortages hit fertilizer output and metal extraction.
records.resilience: Smelter byproduct acid and trade can fill some gaps.
editorialTitles: The Most Important Chemical You Never Hear About
Why Farms and Mines Need Sulfuric Acid

facts.claim: World production in 2022 was estimated at 260 million tonnes.
As of the late 20th century, most of the produced amount (≈60%) was consumed for fertilizers.
Chile, the world's leading producer of copper, required sulfuric acid in about 20% of its copper production as of 2026.
As late as 1940, up to 50% of sulfuric acid manufactured in the United States was produced by chamber process plants.

narration.text: Why we make 260 million tonnes of acid.
That's sulfuric acid output in 2022.
About 60% has gone into fertilizers.
Chile needs it for about 20% of its copper output.
Much of the sulfur comes from refining oil and gas.
Shortages ripple into both food and metals.
That's why an unglamorous acid underpins farms and mines.

records.topic: The Country Making 43% of Industrial Robots
records.coreQuestion: Why has one country become the center of industrial robot production?
records.openingLine: Why China makes 43% of industrial robots.
records.secondBeat: It's also the world's largest robot market.
records.dependency: Car, electronics and metal industries depend on industrial robots and their controllers.
records.mechanism: Robot controllers coordinate motors and sensors to repeat precise movements at high speed.
records.bottleneck: Production is concentrated in a few countries.
records.failureConsequence: Supply disruptions slow new factory lines worldwide.
records.resilience: Japanese, European and Korean makers offer alternatives.
records.expectedConsequence: factory automation projects wait for robots and parts
visualScenes: robot arms welding a car body
editorialTitles: Where the World's Factory Robots Come From
Why China Leads Industrial Robotics

facts.claim: As of 2024, China accounted for 43% of the production of industrial robots in the world.
China is the largest industrial robot market with 154,032 units sold in 2018.
China had the largest operational stock of industrial robots, with 649,447 at the end of 2018.
The biggest customer of industrial robots is automotive industry with 30% market share, then electrical/electronics industry with 25%.
The first two IRB 6 robots were sold to Magnusson in Sweden and were installed in production in January 1974.

narration.text: Why China makes 43% of industrial robots.
It's also the world's largest robot market.
By 2018, it ran 649,447 industrial robots.
Carmakers buy about 30% of all industrial robots.
Electronics makers buy about 25%.
The first IRB 6 robots went into production in 1974.
Each robot depends on precise controllers and motors.
That's why factory automation has its own supply chain.

records.topic: The Bank That Lost $42 Billion in a Day
records.coreQuestion: How did a bank run drain $42 billion from one bank in a single day?
records.openingLine: Why $42 billion fled one bank overnight.
records.secondBeat: In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank faced a run.
records.dependency: Depositors and startups depend on banks staying liquid, and on regulators to resolve failures.
records.mechanism: When depositors rush out, a bank must sell assets; losses on long-term bonds can make it insolvent.
records.bottleneck: Uninsured, concentrated deposits can leave in hours via apps.
records.failureConsequence: SVB failed and was taken over by regulators.
records.resilience: The FDIC took over and guaranteed deposits to stop contagion.
records.expectedConsequence: payrolls freeze until regulators step in
editorialTitles: The Fastest Bank Run in History
Why Deposits Can Vanish in a Day

facts.claim: On March 10, 2023, Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failed after a bank run, marking the third-largest bank failure in United States history.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank

facts.claim: Customers withdrew funds totaling $42 billion by the following day.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank

facts.claim: An additional $100 billion were expected to be withdrawn during Friday.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank

facts.claim: SVB had dramatically increased its holdings of long-term securities since 2021, accounting for them on a hold-to-maturity basis.
facts.source: Wikipedia — Collapse of Silicon Valley Bank

narration.text: Why $42 billion fled one bank overnight.
In March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank faced a run.
It had loaded up on long-term bonds since 2021.
When rates rose, those bonds lost value.
Another $100 billion was expected to leave the next day.
Regulators seized it: the third-largest U.S. bank failure.
That's why deposit insurance is a speed test, not just a promise.

records.topic: The Machine That Overdosed Patients 100 Times
records.coreQuestion: How did a software bug in a radiotherapy machine deliver lethal overdoses?
records.openingLine: Why one machine overdosed patients 100 times over.
records.secondBeat: The Therac-25 treated cancer with radiation beams.
records.dependency: Cancer treatment depends on radiotherapy machines delivering exactly the prescribed dose.
records.mechanism: Software sets beam mode and intensity; hardware interlocks should block dangerous combinations.
records.bottleneck: The design relied on software alone to prevent overdoses.
records.failureConsequence: Race conditions let the machine fire a high-current beam without its safety target.
records.resilience: Hardware interlocks and independent safety analysis became standard.
records.expectedConsequence: patients receive massive overdoses unseen by operators
visualScenes: radiotherapy machine in a treatment room
editorialTitles: The Software Bug That Overdosed Patients
Why Safety Can't Rely on Software Alone

facts.claim: Because of concurrent programming errors (race conditions), it sometimes gave its patients radiation doses that were up to 250 times higher than normal, resulting in death or serious injury.
The high-current electron beam struck the patients with approximately 100 times the intended dose of radiation, and over a narrower area.
He calculated that the applied dose was between 15,000 and 20,000 rad (150…200 Gy) when she should have been dosed with 200 rad (2 Gy).
The Therac-25 was a computer-controlled radiation therapy machine.
A full-body dose of 1000 rad (10 Gy) can be fatal.

narration.text: Why one machine overdosed patients 100 times over.
The Therac-25 treated cancer with radiation beams.
Software race conditions let it fire the wrong beam.
Some doses were up to 250 times higher than normal.
One patient got about 15,000 rad instead of 200.
Its safety depended on software, with no hardware backstop.
That's why life-critical machines need independent interlocks.
